newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS - Ukraine okays plan to raise industry output.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ukraine okays plan to raise industry output.

text.p: Ukraine's parliament adopted a new three-year economic programme on Tuesday aimed at helping flagging industrial enterprises, but it asked unpaid workers to be patient while the economy struggles to turn itself around.

"Maintaining and protecting domestic production, and the national production sector as a whole, holds the central place in our government plan," Prime Minister Lazarenko told parliament, which voted 252-64 in favour of the plan.
But the programme promised no immediate and substantial relief for workers who are owed $1.7 billion in wage arrears.
"We can handle this problem step by step by paying out 200 million hryvnia ($117 million) a month," Lazarenko said.
"But I can't promise that the government can solve this problem immediately."
Economy Minister Vasyl Hureyev said that under the programme, industrial output would grow 1.7 percent in 1997. September industrial output dipped nine percent year-on-year.
"The chief task is to stop a decline in production which has been going on for five years and to get production going again," Hureyev told Reuters.
He said that the government would also implement tax reforms to ease the burden on producers and retain a value-added tax on cigarettes, alcohol and expensive consumer items.
"The current tax system could lead to a national catastrophe," Lazarenko said, adding that President Leonid Kuchma had promised to reform high taxes next year.
Kiev is making progress in taming its post-Soviet economy.
September inflation dropped to two percent from August's 5.7 percent, while June and July had record lows of 0.1 percent, according to government figures.
Annual inflation is expected to total 45-48 percent this year, far below 1995's 182 percent. The 1997 draft budget has targeted an annual inflation rate of 24.9 percent.
But the ex-Soviet republic still has some way to go.
Lazarenko said that only 13 million of Ukraine's 52 million people were working and that government coffers supported 15 million pensioners and paid benefits to 18 million people.
Official data put unemployment at only three million.
"This situation is unique in the world," Lazarenko said.
The government's economic programme also covers the agricultural sector and aims to help large state-run farms that are the country's main food producers.
Government figures based on the 1997 draft budget, to be presented to parliament this week, forecast Ukraine showing economic growth next year for the first time since 1991.
The figures see 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) rising 1.7 percent after a plunge of 11.8 percent in 1995.

Roman Shpek, head of the National Agency for Reconstruction and Development, said Ukraine would also increase industrial output by attracting double the amount of $1.1 billion in foreign investments it has by 1998.
"The government wants to reduce the number of foreign credits and instead receive and increase investment," he said.
Ukraine expects to receive $2.5 billion in foreign credits in 1997, mainly from bodies like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, he said.
